query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Activating a closed‐loop feedback system that dynamically modulates laser parameters during melt pool formation will enhance dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication‐induced defects in additively manufactured high‐entropy alloy components.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloy parts (e.g., CoCrFeNi‐based) produced via standard powder bed fusion with fixed laser parameters.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a closed‐loop feedback control using in situ melt pool and thermal imaging to adjust laser power and scan speed in real time.
generation.conditions: Additive manufacturing of high‐entropy alloys under typical powder bed fusion parameters with the intervention active during melt pool formation. Comparative builds are performed under otherwise identical processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved control of the melt pool dynamics leading to a stabilized melt front that limits keyholing, hot cracking, and uneven cooling, thereby promoting a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Real‐time monitoring enables the system to detect deviations in melt pool behavior and adjust the laser parameters accordingly. This minimizes excessive local energy input and thermal gradients, which are the primary drivers of dimensional deviations and defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with real‐time laser modulation will closely match design geometries, exhibit enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., increased yield and tensile strengths), and display fewer fabrication‐induced defects compared to parts made under fixed-parameter conditions.
generation.baseline: The current powder bed fusion process utilizing preset, fixed laser parameters without in situ feedback control.
generation.boundary: The observed improvements are expected to hold under standard LPBF conditions within the calibrated range of the feedback system. Limitations may arise if sensor resolution or feedback latency falls outside performance expectations, or if non-standard alloy compositions are used.
generation.uncertainty: While the directional improvement is supported by the concept of dynamic process stabilization, the exact magnitude of improvements in machine precision and mechanical performance remains uncertain and will depend on factors such as sensor accuracy, response time, and specific alloy behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a side-by-side experimental comparison by fabricating identical high-entropy alloy components using two processing strategies: one with the standard fixed laser parameter baseline and one with the closed-loop, real-time laser modulation activated. Maintain identical powder bed fusion conditions (e.g., powder type, layer thickness, ambient setup) across both groups.
measurements: Quantitative dimensional analysis via high-resolution 3D scanning.
Mechanical testing (tensile, yield strength, and ductility measurements).
Microstructural characterization (using SEM or optical microscopy to tally defect density, such as cracks and porosity).
In situ thermal imaging data to correlate melt pool stability with output quality.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the group with closed-loop feedback control does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy, mechanical performance, and a reduced defect density compared to the baseline group, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Here, we show how to control the microstructure evolution of additively manufactured stainless steel without relying on mechanical deformation. Using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology, we devise processing strategies to ‘program’ the thermal stability of the as-printed alloy, such that it is possible to decide, a priori, how the material’s microstructure will evolve upon HT. These strategies restore some of the microstructure control capabilities offered by conventional metal processing. More importantly, they allow creating new materials by programming the alloy’s microstructure site-specifically, in 3D, and at high spatial resolution. Site-specific microstructure control of metals is one of the most unique and attractive capabilities of AM. Our strategies showcase an advanced approach to this paradigm by enabling direct control over the evolution of multiple microstructural features at once, broadening the design space of engineering materials with optimized mechanical and physical properties.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters.
